title: Springs and Hooke's law; Stress–strain and force–extension behaviour; Stress, strain and Young modulus
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D06-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; MT01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; MT01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; MT02-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D06-1#N.2b, MT01-1#N.6, D06-1#N.12, MT01-1#N.8, MT01-1#N.9.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Natural length
items.clue: Original, unstretched size of a spring from end to end.

items.label: Tensile strain
items.clue: Extension divided by original length: a ratio with no unit.

items.label: Tensile stress
items.clue: Force divided by the cross-sectional area of a wire, measured in Pa.

items.label: Elastic limit
items.clue: Largest force after which a wire still returns to its original length.

questions.stem: In a lab, a student models a spring as a light spring that obeys Hooke's law. Which statement describes how the spring's force behaves in this model?

options.text: Its force is proportional to its length, measured end to end.
Its force doubles when its extension doubles.
Its force is the same however far it is stretched or compressed.
Its force depends on how fast the attached object is moving.

questions.stem: A student repeats the Young modulus experiment with the same loads on a wire of the same metal and diameter, but only one tenth as long. The extension is read with the same scale. What is the main effect?

options.text: Each extension is ten times smaller, so its percentage uncertainty is ten times larger.
The Young modulus found is ten times smaller.
The stress is ten times larger, so the wire passes its limit of proportionality.
Nothing changes, as the Young modulus is a property of the material.

questions.explanation: Strain is unchanged, so extension ∝ original length. The same reading error is now ten times larger as a fraction of the extension.

questions.stem: A spring that obeys Hooke's law is 15.0 cm long when it supports a 3.0 N load and 18.0 cm long when it supports a 6.0 N load. What is its natural (unloaded) length?
questions.explanation: The extra 3.0 N adds 3.0 cm, so the extension is 1.0 cm per newton. With 3.0 N on, the extension is 3.0 cm: natural length = 15.0 − 3.0 = 12.0 cm.

questions.stem: A cable must carry 12 kN. Steel: working stress 200 MPa, density 7850 kg m⁻³, £1.00 per kg. Aluminium alloy: working stress 100 MPa, density 2700 kg m⁻³, £2.50 per kg. Each cable is made with the smallest safe area. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Aluminium is cheaper and lighter, as it is less dense.
Steel is both cheaper and lighter, as it is stronger.
Steel is cheaper per metre; aluminium is lighter per metre.
They cost the same, as each is used at its own working stress.

questions.explanation: Steel: area = 12 × 10³ ÷ 2.0 × 10⁸ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m², mass 0.47 kg per metre, £0.47. Aluminium: area 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m², 0.32 kg per metre, £0.81.

questions.stem: Two cables are made of the same aluminium alloy and carry the same load. Cable Q is 3 times as long as cable P and has 3 times its diameter. Both obey Hooke's law. What is the extension of Q divided by the extension of P?
questions.explanation: Extension = force × length ÷ (area × Young modulus). Same force and material; length × 3; area × 3² = 9. Ratio = 3/9 = 1/3.
